Part 1 Objectives

  1. Describe lung tumor subtypes (squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, small cell carcinoma, large cell carcinoma), focusing on histologic features, clinical presentation (including paraneoplastic syndromes), central vs. peripheral location, propensity to metastasize, and relative prognosis
  2. Describe lung cancer risk factors and genetic mutations associated with tumor types
PART 1 — Lung Tumor Subtypes

1. Lung Cancer Overview

There are four main types of primary lung carcinoma: squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, small cell carcinoma, and large cell carcinoma.

Historical classification — still useful conceptually — Pathologists used to classify lung cancer simply as small cell (SCLC) vs. non-small cell (NSCLC). At frozen section during surgery, if the diagnosis was small cell, surgeons would stop the operation — small cell is presumed to have already metastasized, so further resection wasn't worthwhile. If non-small cell (regardless of squamous/adeno/large cell), surgery proceeded, since those are not presumed to have already spread. This scheme was formally revised in 2015, but it remains a useful way to think about relative aggressiveness.

Epidemiology & Etiology

  • Lung cancer accounts for 1/3 of cancer deaths in men and is now the leading cause of cancer death in women as well
  • Main etiology: smoking — except adenocarcinoma, which is not strongly smoking-associated
  • Smoking risk is proportional to amount smoked (pack-years); quitting lessens risk but never returns fully to baseline (zero); passive smoke exposure also increases risk
Field effect — Smoking exposes a broad anatomic field (larynx, mouth, lung, etc.) to the same carcinogenic insult. A patient who develops one smoking-related cancer is therefore at elevated risk for a second, separate primary cancer somewhere else in that same exposed field — not just local recurrence or metastasis of the first tumor.

Genetics (General Pattern)

Commonly: an early 3p tumor-suppressor inactivation, with TP53 (tumor suppressor) and KRAS (oncogene) mutations arising later. These are shared to varying degrees across the different histologic subtypes — none is perfectly specific to one type.

2. Squamous Cell Carcinoma

FeatureDetail
Gross locationCentral (around the hilum); often cavitates (necrosis)
MicroscopicIntercellular bridges (fine strands linking desmosomes between cells); keratin pearls (concentric whorls of keratin, minimal nuclei)
Paraneoplastic syndromeParathyroid hormone-related peptide (PTH-rP) → hypercalcemia (can cause hypercalciuria and contribute to kidney stones)
Risk factorSmoking (strong association)
GeneticsMost common lung cancer subtype to carry TP53 mutations; more specifically associated with FGFR1 gene mutation
Intercellular bridges, conceptually — these are the same desmosomal connections that let squamous epithelium (like skin) form a tight protective barrier — nothing passes between the cells. Seeing this feature under the scope is a direct clue to squamous origin.
Squamous cell carcinoma — gross
Central mass with visible cavitation from necrosis. The mottled, more solid-appearing lung tissue adjacent to the mass (upper portion in the original image) was obstructive pneumonia — the tumor blocked the airway, secretions couldn't clear, and infection set in downstream.
Squamous cell carcinoma — histology
Fine strand-like intercellular bridges connect adjacent tumor cells, and a whorled, keratin-rich structure (keratin pearl) with minimal nuclear content is visible — both classic diagnostic features of squamous differentiation.

Basaloid Squamous Cell Carcinoma — A Small-Cell Look-Alike

Basaloid squamous cell carcinoma
The darker, densely packed cells (left) resemble the basal layer of squamous epithelium — small cells with a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, which can superficially resemble small cell carcinoma. The paler, larger cells (right) show the more typical squamous appearance. This is exactly why pathologists lean on immunohistochemical stains (synaptophysin, chromogranin) to distinguish a basaloid squamous pattern from true small cell carcinoma when morphology alone is ambiguous.
Board pearl — Don't rely on nuclear size/N:C ratio alone to call small cell carcinoma — basaloid squamous cell carcinoma can mimic it closely. Neuroendocrine immunostains (synaptophysin, chromogranin, CD56/CD57) are what actually separate the two.

USMLE-Style Question

A 68-year-old man with a 50-pack-year smoking history has a centrally located lung mass with cavitation on imaging. Labs show a serum calcium of 12.8 mg/dL. Biopsy of the mass would most likely show which histologic feature?

A. Keratin pearls and intercellular bridges
B. Neuroendocrine rosettes
C. Glandular formation with mucin production
D. Sheets of cells with no distinguishing differentiation
E. Nuclear molding with scant cytoplasm
Answer: A. A central, cavitating mass with hypercalcemia (from PTH-rP production) is classic for squamous cell carcinoma, which shows keratin pearls and intercellular bridges on histology.

3. Adenocarcinoma

FeatureDetail
Gross locationPeripheral — nearer the pleural surface, distal from the hilum
MicroscopicGlandular formation — invasive glands, spaces lined by tumor cells
Paraneoplastic syndromeMore commonly hematologic: disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC); migratory thrombophlebitis (Trousseau syndrome) — also classic for pancreatic cancer
Risk factorNot strongly associated with smoking (unlike squamous and small cell) — though still a potential risk factor
GeneticsEGFR, ALK (anaplastic lymphoma kinase — targetable with chemotherapy in the ~4–6% of cases that carry it); also ROS1, HER2, c-MET
Propensity to metastasizeOften metastasizes more widely, at an earlier stage, than squamous cell carcinoma
Targetable mutations matter clinically — ALK-positive tumors (a relatively small subset) can be treated with a targeted chemotherapeutic agent, meaningfully changing prognosis — the same principle as HER2-targeted therapy transforming outcomes in HER2-positive breast (and some colon) cancer.
Adenocarcinoma — gross
Tan-white mass located peripherally, near the pleural surface — the classic gross distribution for adenocarcinoma, in contrast to the central location of squamous cell carcinoma.
Adenocarcinoma — histology
Invasive glandular structures — spaces lined by atypical cells — the defining microscopic feature of adenocarcinoma.

Adenocarcinoma in Non-Smokers

  • Incidence has overtaken squamous cell carcinoma as the most common primary lung tumor overall
  • Demographics: younger patients (<45 years), non-smokers
  • Genetics: EGFR and ALK mutations are particularly relevant in this non-smoking population

A Teaching Trap — Diffuse Adenocarcinoma With No Discrete Mass

Diffuse adenocarcinoma (no mass)
This entire lung is diffusely involved by adenocarcinoma — there is no discrete mass anywhere in the specimen. This particular case was clinically mistaken for restrictive lung disease and was only correctly diagnosed as neoplasm at autopsy. Not every lung cancer presents as a lump; a diffuse, pneumonia-like or fibrosis-like pattern is possible and can delay diagnosis.

USMLE-Style Question

A 38-year-old female never-smoker presents with a peripheral lung nodule. Molecular testing reveals an ALK gene rearrangement. Which of the following statements about this finding is most accurate?

A. ALK rearrangements are seen in a minority of adenocarcinomas but are clinically important because they can be targeted with specific chemotherapy
B. This mutation is more common in squamous cell carcinoma than adenocarcinoma
C. This mutation precludes any targeted therapy options
D. This finding indicates the tumor is of neuroendocrine origin
E. ALK mutations are associated primarily with heavy smoking history
Answer: A. ALK rearrangements occur in a relatively small subset of adenocarcinomas (particularly in younger, non-smoking patients) but are clinically significant because targeted ALK inhibitor therapy is available, similar in concept to HER2-targeted therapy in breast cancer.

4. Small Cell Carcinoma

FeatureDetail
ClassificationA neuroendocrine carcinoma — same family as carcinoid and large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma
Gross locationOften central
MicroscopicHigh N:C ratio (scant cytoplasm, abundant nucleus); nuclear molding (adjacent nuclei push against and conform to each other's shape); high mitotic rate; necrosis
Paraneoplastic syndromesACTH → Cushing syndrome; SIADH → hyponatremia from inappropriate ADH
Risk factorSmoking (strong association, like squamous cell)
GeneticsRB (retinoblastoma) mutations much more common than in NSCLC; KRAS mutations much rarer than in NSCLC
Neuroendocrine markersChromogranin, synaptophysin, CD56 (CD57 also reported in some literature)
Propensity to metastasizeHighest of all subtypes — the basis for the old "small cell = stop the surgery" teaching point
Necrosis isn't specific — squamous cell carcinoma can also show necrosis/cavitation, so necrosis alone doesn't distinguish subtypes. What IS distinguishing for small cell is the combination of high N:C ratio + nuclear molding, confirmed with neuroendocrine immunostains when morphology is ambiguous (e.g., vs. basaloid squamous cell carcinoma, Section 2).
Small cell carcinoma — necrosis
Pink, amorphous necrotic debris amid sheets of small, hyperchromatic tumor cells — reflecting the aggressive, rapidly-growing nature of this tumor, which frequently outgrows its blood supply.
Small cell carcinoma — nuclear molding
Adjacent tumor nuclei are pressed against one another and conform to each other's shape (nuclear molding) — a classic, distinguishing feature of small cell carcinoma, alongside the markedly high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio visible throughout the field.

USMLE-Style Question

A 61-year-old smoker with a central lung mass is found to have hyponatremia with inappropriately concentrated urine and normal volume status. Biopsy shows sheets of small cells with scant cytoplasm and nuclear molding. Which paraneoplastic mechanism best explains the hyponatremia?

A. Ectopic ADH production causing SIADH
B. Ectopic PTH-related peptide production
C. Ectopic ACTH production causing Cushing syndrome
D. Migratory thrombophlebitis
E. Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome
Answer: A. Small cell carcinoma classically produces ectopic ADH, causing SIADH — euvolemic hyponatremia with inappropriately concentrated urine — consistent with the tumor's neuroendocrine hormone-producing capability.

USMLE-Style Question

Which genetic finding would be most useful in distinguishing small cell carcinoma from non-small cell lung carcinoma?

A. RB mutation, much more common in small cell carcinoma
B. TP53 mutation, present equally in both
C. KRAS mutation, much more common in small cell carcinoma
D. EGFR mutation, equally common in both
E. FGFR1 mutation, more common in small cell carcinoma
Answer: A. RB (retinoblastoma) mutations are much more common in small cell carcinoma than in non-small cell lung carcinoma, while KRAS mutations are much rarer in small cell carcinoma compared to NSCLC — the reverse of option B.

5. Large Cell Carcinoma

Large cell carcinoma is essentially a diagnosis of exclusion — a catch-all category for tumors that show no features of squamous, glandular, or neuroendocrine differentiation on standard evaluation.

Practical framing — Ask: do I see keratin pearls or intercellular bridges (squamous)? Glandular spaces (adenocarcinoma)? High N:C ratio with nuclear molding, or positive neuroendocrine stains (small cell/neuroendocrine)? If the answer to all of these is no, the tumor falls into large cell carcinoma by default. As immunohistochemical and molecular techniques improve, some tumors previously labeled "large cell" may eventually be reclassified into one of the other categories.

USMLE-Style Question

A poorly differentiated lung tumor is biopsied. Staining is negative for squamous markers, shows no glandular architecture, and neuroendocrine markers (synaptophysin, chromogranin) are negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A. Small cell carcinoma
B. Carcinoid tumor
C. Adenocarcinoma in situ
D. Large cell carcinoma
E. Squamous cell carcinoma, basaloid variant
Answer: D. Large cell carcinoma is a diagnosis of exclusion, applied when a lung tumor lacks squamous, glandular, or neuroendocrine differentiation on histology and immunohistochemistry.

6. Precursor Lesions

None of the following are cancer themselves — they represent points along a progression pathway that can develop into invasive carcinoma with further genetic hits.

Squamous dysplasia / carcinoma in situChronic irritation (e.g., cigarette smoke) → squamous metaplasia of bronchial epithelium → dysplasia (abnormal growth) → carcinoma in situ, where cells look fully neoplastic but have not yet invaded the basement membrane
Atypical adenomatous hyperplasia (AAH)Hyperplasia (too many cells) with glandular ("adenoma") architecture that looks atypical, but is not yet carcinoma
Adenocarcinoma in situ (AIS)Older term: bronchioloalveolar carcinoma. Looks like adenocarcinoma but has not invaded
Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia (DIPNECH)A possible precursor/risk factor for small cell carcinoma and carcinoid tumors
Remember the two defining features of true cancer — invasion and metastasis. Every lesion in this table lacks at least the invasion component (by definition), which is exactly what separates a "precursor" from "carcinoma."

Adenocarcinoma In Situ vs. Type II Pneumocyte Hyperplasia — A Key Distinction

AIS shows growth of tall, columnar tumor cells along normal alveolar septa (a growth pattern called lepidic growth), with no fibrosis and no other reason for the pneumocytes to be reactive. By contrast, Type II pneumocyte hyperplasia is a reactive process — tall cuboidal cells lining alveoli, but occurring specifically because of an underlying insult, with associated fibrosis as evidence of that ongoing injury/repair process. Historically, patients with unrecognized AIS often presented as a "pneumonia" that never resolved with treatment — the biopsy taken to investigate the non-resolving infiltrate is what ultimately revealed the diagnosis.

Type II pneumocyte hyperplasia (reactive, NOT neoplastic)
Tall, reactive cuboidal cells line the alveolar septa, and — unlike AIS — there is accompanying fibrosis, reflecting a genuine underlying reparative/inflammatory process rather than a neoplastic proliferation growing along otherwise normal architecture.
Critical caveat — AIS can hide an invasive component — Because a lesion labeled "adenocarcinoma in situ" can co-exist with a genuinely invasive focus elsewhere in the same tumor, pathologists must sample carefully. The image below is from a patient whose lesion was called AIS/bronchioloalveolar carcinoma at first glance — but a separate area of the same tumor showed clear invasion.
Invasive adenocarcinoma arising with an AIS component
A blood vessel (center) contains small glandular structures within its lumen — direct evidence of vascular invasion by tumor cells. This is why an apparent "in situ" diagnosis always requires careful, thorough sampling: an invasive focus can be present elsewhere in the same lesion.

USMLE-Style Question

A lung biopsy shows tall columnar cells growing along otherwise normal, non-fibrotic alveolar septa, with no evidence of stromal or vascular invasion elsewhere in multiple sampled sections. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A. Type II pneumocyte hyperplasia
B. Usual interstitial pneumonia
C. Small cell carcinoma
D. Diffuse alveolar damage
E. Adenocarcinoma in situ
Answer: E. Growth of tall columnar cells along normal (non-fibrotic) alveolar septa without invasion is the defining pattern of adenocarcinoma in situ (lepidic growth), distinguishing it from type II pneumocyte hyperplasia, which occurs in a background of fibrosis/reactive change.

7. Clinical Features & Paraneoplastic Syndromes

Rather than memorizing a list, work through the anatomy: think about what structure is involved and what a tumor growing there, or blocking that structure, would cause.

CoughCentral airway irritation
HemoptysisErosion into an airway from a necrotic, bleeding tumor
Chest painExtension into the pleura or chest wall (can include rib involvement)
Pneumonia / abscessAirway obstruction impairing normal clearance
Lipoid pneumoniaAccumulation of macrophages (a downstream consequence of obstruction)
Pleural effusionMalignant effusion if tumor erodes through the pleural surface
HoarsenessRecurrent laryngeal nerve involvement
DysphagiaEsophageal invasion (esophagus sits right behind the trachea/lung)
Diaphragm paralysisPhrenic nerve involvement
Pericarditis/tamponadeInvasion into the pericardial sac/heart
SVC syndromeApical tumor invading and compressing the superior vena cava → impaired venous return from head/neck/upper extremities, causing congestion
Horner syndromeApical tumor invading the sympathetic nerve ganglia
Pancoast tumor — the term for an apical lung tumor causing either SVC syndrome or Horner syndrome (or both) via local invasion at the lung apex.

Horner Syndrome (Mnemonic Kemp Uses Himself)

EnophthalmosPosterior displacement of the eye within the orbit
PtosisDrooping upper eyelid
MiosisConstricted pupil
AnhidrosisDecreased/absent facial sweating
Apical (Pancoast) tumor with downstream obstructive pneumonia
The apex of the lung (top) shows tumor extending outward — given the location, adenocarcinoma would be the most likely single guess among the major subtypes. A separate, more centrally-located mass lower in the specimen (thought to be squamous cell carcinoma in this case) has caused airway obstruction, and the surrounding denser, more solid-appearing lung tissue represents secondary obstructive pneumonia — not tumor itself.

Paraneoplastic Syndromes — Full List

ADH (SIADH)Small cell
ACTH (Cushing syndrome)Small cell
PTH-related peptide (hypercalcemia)Squamous cell (most classic association)
Calcitonin, gonadotropins, serotonin/bradykininVarious — serotonin/bradykinin more classically carcinoid
Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndromeBlocks neuromuscular transmission → proximal muscle weakness; classically small cell
Acanthosis nigricansBrown/velvety discoloration of axillary skin; also classically associated with gastric cancer and diabetes
Trousseau syndromeMigratory thrombophlebitis; classic for both adenocarcinoma of lung and pancreatic cancer
Hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy (HPOA)Clubbing/rounding of the distal fingers; can also be hereditary/idiopathic, so is not by itself proof of malignancy
Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)Widespread clotting, consuming clotting factors — more associated with adenocarcinoma
Hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy
Bulbous enlargement of the distal fingers (clubbing). This finding can also occur as a benign hereditary trait unrelated to malignancy, so digital clubbing alone should prompt a broader work-up, not an automatic cancer diagnosis.
Acanthosis nigricans
Brown, velvety hyperpigmentation of the axillary skin. While associated with lung cancer as a paraneoplastic phenomenon, this finding is seen far more often in the context of diabetes/insulin resistance in routine clinical practice.

USMLE-Style Question

A patient with a lung mass at the apex develops ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis on the same side of the face, along with facial and arm swelling. Which combination of structures has most likely been affected by tumor invasion?

A. Recurrent laryngeal nerve only
B. Phrenic nerve only
C. Sympathetic chain and the superior vena cava
D. Esophagus and pericardium
E. Vagus nerve and thoracic duct
Answer: C. Ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis constitute Horner syndrome, from sympathetic ganglion invasion, while facial/arm swelling suggests concurrent SVC compression — together the classic presentation of an apical (Pancoast) tumor affecting both structures.

USMLE-Style Question

A patient with newly diagnosed lung cancer develops recurrent episodes of pain and redness along superficial veins in different locations over several weeks, with no clear infectious source. Which term describes this finding, and with which lung cancer subtype is it most classically associated?

A. Virchow node; squamous cell carcinoma
B. Lambert-Eaton syndrome; small cell carcinoma
C. Horner syndrome; large cell carcinoma
D. SIADH; carcinoid tumor
E. Trousseau syndrome (migratory thrombophlebitis); adenocarcinoma
Answer: E. Migratory thrombophlebitis (Trousseau syndrome) reflects a hypercoagulable paraneoplastic state, classically associated with adenocarcinoma of the lung (and pancreatic adenocarcinoma).

8. Carcinoid Tumor & the Neuroendocrine Spectrum

FeatureDetail
DemographicsYounger patients, <40 years — similar to adenocarcinoma-in-nonsmokers demographic pattern
AssociationCan be part of multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) syndrome
GrossPolyp or plaque within the bronchus; can expand outward around the airway lumen — described as a "collar-button" lesion
Microscopic (typical carcinoid)Round, bland nuclei — little to no pleomorphism, little to no mitotic activity; classic "salt and pepper" chromatin
Clinical (local)Intraluminal growth → cough, hemoptysis, downstream obstruction → pulmonary infection
Carcinoid syndromeDiarrhea, flushing, cyanosis — from serotonin reaching systemic circulation; classically a GI carcinoid phenomenon, rare for pulmonary carcinoid specifically (often requires a right-sided heart lesion/shunt to bypass hepatic metabolism of serotonin)
Naming logic — "Carcinoid" reflects the historical idea that this tumor is "cancer-like" but generally much less aggressive than a true carcinoma — hence a distinct, softer name.

Neuroendocrine Aggressiveness Spectrum

Typical carcinoid (lowest grade) → Atypical carcinoid → Large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma → Small cell carcinoma (highest grade)

Typical carcinoid is capable of invasion and metastasis but is very low-grade malignancy. Atypical carcinoid shows more nuclear irregularity/pleomorphism and some mitotic activity — an intermediate step toward the more aggressive large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma and, at the far end, small cell carcinoma.

USMLE-Style Question

A 32-year-old presents with recurrent cough and hemoptysis. Bronchoscopy reveals a polypoid endobronchial lesion. Biopsy shows round, bland nuclei with finely granular ('salt and pepper') chromatin and minimal mitotic activity. Which of the following best describes this tumor's expected biological behavior?

A. Extremely aggressive, high risk of early widespread metastasis, similar to small cell carcinoma
B. Capable of invasion and metastasis, but low-grade malignancy
C. Entirely benign with zero metastatic potential
D. Behavior identical to large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma
E. Always associated with carcinoid syndrome
Answer: B. This describes a typical carcinoid tumor — capable of local invasion and even metastasis, but representing a low-grade malignancy at the most indolent end of the pulmonary neuroendocrine tumor spectrum, well below atypical carcinoid, large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma, and small cell carcinoma in aggressiveness.

9. Other Lung Tumors

HamartomaBenign nodule of mature cartilage admixed with fat, fibrous tissue, and blood vessels. Once thought to be a developmental malformation, but is actually clonal (implying a neoplastic, though very low-grade, process). Classic incidental finding on chest imaging.
Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM)Occurs in young females; involves perivascular epithelioid cells expressing both smooth muscle and melanocytic markers; associated with loss-of-function mutation in TSC2; causes emphysema-like changes in the lung.
Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumorTypically seen in children; can present with fever, chest pain, hemoptysis; composed of fibroblasts/myofibroblasts in a background of chronic inflammation; can carry an ALK gene alteration (an interesting parallel to ALK in adenocarcinoma).

Other soft tissue and hematopoietic tumors (e.g., leiomyoma, lymphoma) can also arise in or involve the lung — worth knowing they exist as a broader category, without needing exhaustive detail on each.

USMLE-Style Question

A 34-year-old woman presents with progressive dyspnea. CT shows diffuse cystic changes throughout both lungs resembling emphysema. Biopsy reveals proliferation of perivascular epithelioid cells expressing both smooth muscle actin and melanocytic markers. Which gene is most likely affected in this condition?

A. ALK
B. EGFR
C. TSC2
D. TP53
E. BAP1
Answer: C. This presentation is classic for lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM), which occurs in young women and is associated with loss-of-function mutations in TSC2, causing proliferation of perivascular epithelioid cells (PEComas) with combined smooth muscle and melanocytic marker expression.

PART 2 — Complications, Metastasis & Pleural Disease

11. Complications of Pulmonary Neoplasms

Same approach as Part 1's clinical features section: use anatomy and pathophysiology to reason through presentations rather than memorizing an isolated list.

DeathLung cancer remains a leading cause of cancer death in both men and women
Airway obstruction→ atelectasis and/or pneumonia downstream
Hemorrhage into the airwayFrom a necrotic mass eroding into the airway lumen — can range from hemoptysis to (rarely) fatal exsanguination
Pro-thrombotic stateContributes to DIC, migratory thrombophlebitis (especially adenocarcinoma)
Malignant pleural effusionTumor erosion through the pleural surface (often adenocarcinoma, given its peripheral location) → fluid accumulation → subsequent pleural adhesions/scarring
Neurologic effectsHorner syndrome (sympathetic ganglion invasion)
Invasion of surrounding structuresEsophagus (dysphagia), heart/pericardium
Pathologic fracturesFrom metastatic spread to bone
Hormone productionACTH, ADH, and others (paraneoplastic)
CachexiaHistorically attributed simply to the tumor "using up" nutrients, but the actual mechanism is more complex (cytokine-mediated systemic catabolic state)
Practical takeaway — When you encounter a case, ask: where is this tumor anatomically, and what structures does that location put at risk? A patient can present anywhere from a completely incidental imaging finding to a full-blown emergency (massive hemoptysis, tamponade, SVC syndrome) depending purely on location and local extension — not necessarily on histologic subtype.

USMLE-Style Question

A patient with known lung adenocarcinoma develops sudden-onset shortness of breath. Imaging reveals a new pleural effusion. Thoracentesis is performed. Beyond symptomatic relief, what is the most important next step for the fluid obtained?

A. Discard the fluid after symptomatic relief is achieved
B. Send the fluid for cytologic examination to determine if it represents a malignant effusion
C. Culture only for aerobic bacteria
D. No further workup is needed since the patient has known cancer
E. Test only for glucose and pH
Answer: B. Any new pleural effusion in a cancer patient should be evaluated cytologically to determine whether it represents a malignant effusion (tumor cells present) versus another cause, since this affects staging, prognosis, and management.

12. Metastatic Spread To/From Lung

General principle — Carcinomas (which is what all four major lung cancer subtypes are) tend to spread via lymphatics; sarcomas tend to spread hematogenously. Since squamous cell, adenocarcinoma, small cell, and large cell carcinoma are all carcinomas, lymphatic spread is the expected primary route.

Lymphatic Spread From Lung Carcinoma

  • Nodal groups: carina, mediastinum, neck (scalene), and clavicular nodes
  • Left supraclavicular nodal involvement — known as Virchow node — is characteristic of an underlying lung (or other visceral) neoplasm. A palpable left supraclavicular node in a smoker should prompt concern for this, though reactive/benign causes are also possible on biopsy, so tissue diagnosis (e.g., fine-needle aspiration) still matters before assuming malignancy.

Metastases TO the Lung

The lung is a common site for metastasis from other primary tumors, given the volume of blood flow it receives (the entire cardiac output passes through the pulmonary circulation). Different primary tumors have different preferred metastatic sites — e.g., colon cancer preferentially favors the liver but can also spread to lung.

Multiple pulmonary metastases ("cannonball" pattern)
Numerous discrete, round, well-circumscribed white nodules scattered throughout the lung parenchyma — the classic "cannonball" appearance of hematogenous metastases (in this teaching set, examples included metastatic colon cancer and chondrosarcoma). This pattern reflects seeding via the pulmonary vasculature rather than lymphatic spread — the opposite direction of travel from a primary lung carcinoma spreading out to lymph nodes.

USMLE-Style Question

A 58-year-old male smoker is found to have a firm, non-tender lymph node just above the left clavicle. Fine-needle aspiration is performed. This nodal location and clinical scenario is classically referred to by which eponym, and what does its presence classically suggest?

A. Sister Mary Joseph node; gastric cancer
B. Virchow node; underlying visceral (e.g., lung) malignancy
C. Delphian node; thyroid cancer
D. Krukenberg node; ovarian metastasis
E. Troisier sign; pancreatic cancer only
Answer: B. Left supraclavicular lymphadenopathy is termed Virchow node and is classically associated with an underlying visceral malignancy, particularly gastric or lung cancer, reached via lymphatic spread through the thoracic duct.

13. Mediastinal Tumors by Location

Location within the mediastinum meaningfully narrows the differential diagnosis — largely because it reflects which normal structures/organs are present in each compartment.

AnteriorPosteriorMiddle
ThymomaNeurogenic tumors (e.g., schwannoma — sympathetic chain)Bronchogenic cyst
Teratoma (can occur anywhere in the midline)LymphomaPericardial cyst
Lymphoma (can occur anywhere lymph nodes exist)Metastatic tumorLymphoma
Thyroid/parathyroid tumorsBronchogenic cyst
Metastatic tumorGastroenteric hernia
Reasoning strategy — Rather than memorizing this table by rote, think about which normal organs/structures live in each compartment: thymus and thyroid sit anteriorly; the sympathetic chain and nerve roots run posteriorly along the spine; the trachea/bronchi and pericardium sit centrally in the middle mediastinum. The tumor types simply follow from the tissue that's normally there (plus lymphoma and metastases, which can occur essentially anywhere lymphatic tissue or blood supply reaches).

USMLE-Style Question

A CT scan reveals an anterior mediastinal mass in a 45-year-old with myasthenia gravis symptoms. Which tumor is most likely?

A. Schwannoma
B. Bronchogenic cyst
C. Thymoma
D. Pericardial cyst
E. Neurogenic tumor
Answer: C. Thymoma is an anterior mediastinal mass classically associated with myasthenia gravis (thymic tumors are found in a substantial proportion of myasthenia gravis patients, and thymectomy is part of management in appropriate cases).

14. Pleural Effusions

A pleural effusion is simply fluid (or another substance) accumulating in the pleural space — the composition ranges from watery/clear to frankly bloody, and the terminology reflects this composition.

CategoryTypes
Non-inflammatoryHydrothorax (transudate — e.g., congestive heart failure); chylothorax (lymphatic/thoracic duct obstruction, causing lymph to leak into the pleural space)
InflammatorySerous (watery, e.g., viral); serofibrinous; fibrinous (more protein-rich, from an acute inflammatory process); purulent (neutrophil-rich, from bacterial infection); hemorrhagic (red blood cells present, classically raises concern for malignancy)

Causes and Their Typical Fluid Character

Congestive heart failureTransudate (hydrothorax)
Bacterial invasion (from lung or bloodstream)Exudate (neutrophil-rich)
NeoplasmExudate
Pulmonary infarctionExudate — necrosis at the pleural surface triggers inflammation, neutrophils, fibrin deposition
ViralCould be transudate or exudate
Connective tissue disease (SLE, RA)Serositis — can affect pleura, pericardium, and peritoneum simultaneously; can also contribute to restrictive lung disease from parenchymal scarring
Point to ponder — which effusion type is least/most likely to cause pleural adhesions, and why? Adhesions (scarring) form when material cannot be fully cleared/resolved. A watery transudate (hydrothorax from CHF) or a simple viral serous effusion is easily resorbed → least likely to scar. Fibrinous, purulent, or hemorrhagic effusions contain far more protein/cellular debris that is harder to clear → most likely to organize into adhesions. Practically: finding pleural adhesions at autopsy raises suspicion for a prior bacterial pneumonia (or worse); a hemorrhagic effusion raises concern for malignancy.
Fibrinous pleuritis (HSV pleuritis case)
A thin, fibrinous coating is visible on the pleural surface — reminiscent of the "bread and butter" appearance classically described for fibrinous pericarditis, just on the pleura instead. In this specific case, the underlying cause was herpes simplex virus, identified on histology by characteristic viral inclusions (Cowdry A-type inclusions resembling CMV, and Cowdry B-type multinucleated cells with a smudged chromatin appearance).

USMLE-Style Question

At autopsy, a patient is found to have dense fibrous pleural adhesions bilaterally. Which of the following effusion types would most plausibly have led to this finding over time?

A. Transudative hydrothorax from heart failure
B. Simple viral serous effusion
C. Purulent (empyema) effusion from bacterial pneumonia
D. Chylothorax from lymphatic obstruction
E. None of the above can cause adhesions
Answer: C. A purulent effusion (empyema) from bacterial infection contains abundant protein, neutrophils, and cellular debris that is difficult to fully clear, making organization into fibrous pleural adhesions much more likely than with a simple transudate or watery viral effusion.

USMLE-Style Question

A patient develops a pleural effusion following a pulmonary embolism with infarction. What is the expected fluid character, and why?

A. Transudate, because infarction does not provoke inflammation
B. Exudate, because necrosis at the pleural surface triggers an inflammatory response with fibrin deposition
C. Chylothorax, because the thoracic duct is obstructed
D. Pure transudate identical to CHF-related effusions
E. No effusion is expected with pulmonary infarction
Answer: B. Pulmonary infarction causes tissue necrosis, which triggers inflammation at the pleural surface with neutrophil infiltration and fibrin deposition — producing an exudative effusion, not a transudate.

15. Pneumothorax

DescriptionAir within the pleural cavity
CausesSpontaneous rupture of a bleb/bulla (classically young males with subpleural blebs); secondary to trauma (stab wound, rib fracture)
TypesTension vs. non-tension
ComplicationsCompression of the lung → airway/vascular obstruction, atelectasis, secondary pneumonia
Tension pneumothorax mechanism — "ball-and-valve" — On inspiration, air escapes into the pleural cavity; on expiration, the defect closes and traps that air inside. Each breath adds more trapped air without any way out, progressively compressing the lung (and eventually mediastinal structures/venous return). This is a life-threatening emergency requiring urgent needle/catheter decompression — a maneuver simple enough that, in trauma cases (e.g., motor vehicle accidents), it's common to find bilateral chest catheters already placed by the time of autopsy, reflecting how quickly this was addressed during resuscitation.
Gunshot wound — pneumothorax + hemothorax
Three findings in one film: a radiopaque bullet fragment; one hemithorax that is diffusely blacked-out from absent lung markings (pneumothorax — air where lung tissue should be); and the opposite hemithorax that is diffusely whited-out (hemothorax — blood filling the pleural space). A single penetrating injury produced both findings simultaneously, on opposite sides of the chest.

USMLE-Style Question

A trauma patient with a stab wound to the chest develops progressive hypotension, distended neck veins, and tracheal deviation away from the affected side. Breath sounds are absent on the affected side. What is the most likely underlying mechanism?

A. Simple non-tension pneumothorax with no hemodynamic effect
B. Cardiac tamponade from pericardial effusion
C. Chylothorax from thoracic duct injury
D. A ball-and-valve mechanism allowing air into the pleural space on inspiration but preventing its escape on expiration
E. Hemothorax alone without pleural air
Answer: D. This presentation (hypotension, JVD, tracheal deviation, absent breath sounds) is classic for tension pneumothorax, caused by a one-way ball-and-valve mechanism that lets air enter the pleural space with each breath but prevents it from escaping, progressively compressing the lung and mediastinum — a true emergency requiring immediate decompression.

16. Mesothelioma

FeatureDetail
EtiologyAsbestos exposure (shipyards, insulation work, mining) — the association is strong enough that, practically speaking, a mesothelioma diagnosis should prompt an asbestos exposure history "until proven otherwise"
GeneticsMost commonly associated with BAP1 — a tumor suppressor gene involved in DNA repair
GrossArises in the pleural cavity (can also involve the pericardial or peritoneal cavity); classically encases/surrounds the lung rather than forming a discrete mass — gross appearance alone can be strongly suggestive
MicroscopicCan be epithelial (looks like carcinoma), sarcomatous (spindle cell), or both (biphasic)
Diagnosis requires special stains — Even with a classic gross appearance, confirming mesothelioma (and distinguishing it from other possibilities, like a primary or metastatic carcinoma involving the pleura) requires specific immunohistochemical stains performed by surgical pathology — this is not a call to make on gross appearance or routine H&E alone.

Case 1 — The Mimicker

At autopsy, the pleural surface showed shaggy, red-brown material that initially looked like an old, organizing hemorrhage or resolving pneumonia process. A section submitted for histology, however, revealed mesothelioma.

Malignant mesothelioma — gross (Case 1)
Shaggy, red-brown tissue coating the pleural cavity, initially suspected to represent an old, organizing hemorrhagic or inflammatory process rather than tumor — underscoring that mesothelioma doesn't always look classic grossly.
Biphasic mesothelioma + incidental bone marrow embolus
This field shows both components of a biphasic mesothelioma — glandular, epithelioid-appearing nests alongside spindled, sarcomatoid areas. As an aside unrelated to the tumor itself, the upper right of this same field contains a bone marrow embolus (fat vacuoles admixed with hematopoietic cells within a vessel) — an incidental finding with no connection to the mesothelioma, included as a reminder that unrelated findings can turn up in the same slide.

Case 2 — Classic Gross Encasement

A second autopsy case showed the more textbook gross presentation: no mass identified in the hilum of the affected lung — instead, the entire lung was covered by a layer of tan-pink tumor tissue. The contralateral (uninvolved) lung was unremarkable, providing a clear side-by-side comparison.

Malignant mesothelioma encasing the lung — gross (Case 2)
Direct comparison of both lungs at autopsy: one lung (left in the image) is essentially normal, while the other is entirely covered by a thick rind of tan-white tumor tissue completely encasing the pulmonary parenchyma — the classic gross appearance of malignant mesothelioma, with no discrete mass and no hilar lesion identified separately.
Biphasic mesothelioma — histology (Case 2)
Glandular, epithelioid-appearing tumor nests are visible alongside a spindled, fibrous-appearing sarcomatoid component within the same tumor — confirming a biphasic mesothelioma, the same pattern seen in Case 1.
Real-world lesson from both cases — "A lot of times the things you encounter out in the real world don't really read the books." Case 1 looked like an old hemorrhage/inflammatory process, not a tumor. Both required special stains from surgical pathology to confirm the diagnosis rather than being called from gross appearance or routine histology alone. Don't expect every real case to hand you the textbook picture.

USMLE-Style Question

An autopsy reveals a lung entirely encased by a thick rind of tan-white tumor tissue, with no discrete mass identifiable in the hilum. Histology shows both glandular epithelioid areas and spindled sarcomatoid areas within the same tumor. What is the most likely occupational history for this patient?

A. Long-term tobacco farming
B. Working in a bakery with high flour dust exposure
C. Coal mining exclusively
D. Shipyard work or insulation installation with asbestos exposure
E. No occupational exposure is relevant to this diagnosis
Answer: D. This gross and histologic picture (lung-encasing tumor with biphasic epithelioid/sarcomatoid histology) is classic for malignant mesothelioma, which should prompt an asbestos exposure history — classically shipyard work, insulation work, or mining — "until proven otherwise."

USMLE-Style Question

Which tumor suppressor gene, involved in DNA repair, is most commonly associated with malignant mesothelioma?

A. TP53
B. RB1
C. TSC2
D. APC
E. BAP1
Answer: E. BAP1 (BRCA1-associated protein 1), a tumor suppressor gene involved in DNA repair, is the gene most commonly associated with malignant mesothelioma.

18. Master High-Yield Pearls (Both Parts)

  • Central lung tumors: squamous cell, small cell. Peripheral: adenocarcinoma.
  • Most aggressive/highest metastatic potential: small cell carcinoma. Diagnosis of exclusion: large cell carcinoma.
  • Targetable mutations matter clinically: EGFR/ALK in adenocarcinoma (especially non-smokers) — a reason to always check genetics, since it can change treatment and prognosis.
  • Paraneoplastic hormone pairings: Squamous → PTH-rP (hypercalcemia). Small cell → ACTH (Cushing) and ADH (SIADH). Adenocarcinoma → hypercoagulable state (DIC, Trousseau syndrome).
  • Anatomy drives clinical presentation for both primary tumor effects and complications — trace the structures adjacent to where the tumor sits (nerves, esophagus, heart, great vessels) to predict presentation, rather than memorizing symptom lists in isolation.
  • Pancoast tumor = apical tumor → Horner syndrome and/or SVC syndrome via local invasion.
  • Carcinomas spread via lymphatics (Virchow node = left supraclavicular); sarcomas spread hematogenously; the lung itself is a common site of hematogenous metastasis from elsewhere ("cannonball" pattern).
  • Pleural fluid character reflects its cause: transudate = CHF; exudate = infection, neoplasm, infarction; hemorrhagic = concern for malignancy; more protein/cellular debris = more likely to organize into adhesions.
  • Tension pneumothorax is a ball-and-valve emergency — recognize it clinically (hypotension, JVD, tracheal deviation, absent breath sounds) and treat immediately with decompression.
  • Mesothelioma = asbestos + BAP1 + encases the lung + epithelial/sarcomatous/biphasic — but still needs special stains to confirm, and real cases don't always look textbook grossly.
  • Real-world reminder repeated throughout both lectures: pathology doesn't always match the textbook picture — atypical presentations (diffuse adenocarcinoma with no mass, mesothelioma mimicking old hemorrhage) are exactly why careful sampling and special stains matter.
